title: Pearls: Second Best Thing About Oysters
summary: Josh and Chuck explore pearls: how they form as an irritant-driven defense by mollusks, the difference between nacreous true pearls and non-nacreous pearls (queen conch, melo), the history of pearl diving and pearl use from ancient Persia and Susa through Cleopatra, Elizabeth I and medieval sumptuary laws, the late-19th-century Gaston Vives oyster farming, Japanese pearl cultivation by Kokichi Mikimoto, Tokichi Nishikawa and Tatsuei Misawa (the Nishikawa method), the ethics and ecology of pearl farming, and famous pearls such as La Peregrina. The episode closes with listener mail about the SYSK 5K event.

segments.title: Opening banter and listener suggestion
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, credit listener Jamie Boo for the pearls suggestion, and chat about the Steinbeck novel The Pearl and Of Mice and Men.

segments.title: What pearls are and how they form
segments.summary: Pearls can come from many mollusks; they form when an irritant such as a grain of sand or parasite is coated by the mollusk. Pearls are rare, about one in ten thousand mollusks. True pearls are made of nacre (aragonite plus conchiolin), the same material as mother of pearl.

segments.title: Non-nacreous pearls and where pearls come from
segments.summary: Non-nacreous pearls are made of calcite-based calcareous concretions and come from mollusks like the queen conch and melo sea snail. Freshwater mussels in the Tennessee River and saltwater oysters in places like the Gulf of California and Japan produce true pearls.

segments.title: Pearl diving
segments.summary: Pearls come from deep water where flow is slow. Pearl divers historically free-dived to depths of around fifty meters holding their breath for minutes.

segments.title: Ancient and medieval pearl history
segments.summary: Pearls were prized by ancient cultures and nobility. The oldest known pearl necklace, from about 2,300 to 2,400 years ago at Susa in Iran, had 216 pearls. Pearls were used in medicine, Cleopatra's vinegar legend is recounted, and medieval sumptuary laws restricted pearl wearing.

segments.title: Colonial pearl trade, Elizabeth I, and early oyster farming
segments.summary: Colonizers harvested pearls for Europe; Elizabeth I was said to wear thousands of pearls. In the late nineteenth century Gaston Vives began large-scale oyster farming in Mexico to produce pearls naturally, yielding four to fourteen percent pearls per hundred oysters.

segments.title: Cultured pearls in Japan and the Nishikawa method
segments.summary: Early culturing in China used molds for blister pearls. William Saville-Kent in Australia pursued culturing but only achieved blister pearls. In Japan, Kokichi Mikimoto worked with Kakichi Mitsukuri; Tokichi Nishikawa, a student of Mitsukuri, and carpenter Tatsuei Misawa developed the technique of implanting nuclei to create true cultured pearls, known as the Nishikawa method.

segments.title: Imitation pearls and Mikimoto's legacy
segments.summary: Mikimoto aimed to democratize pearls, and cultured pearls are less expensive but genuine. Imitation pearls became popular after the Depression, and Jackie Kennedy's famous necklace was reportedly artificial, likely glass.

segments.title: Modern pearl farming, types, and ethics
segments.summary: Modern cultured pearls include Akoya, South Sea, Tahitian (black-lip oyster) and freshwater types. Baroque pearls are non-spherical. Cultivation takes ten to eighteen months, with few oysters producing high-quality pearls, and pearls are harvested by killing the oysters. Pearl farming is debated ethically but may benefit water quality and reduce overfishing.

segments.title: Famous and large pearls
segments.summary: A 75-pound pearl valued at about 100 million dollars was kept under a bed in the Philippines and never sold. La Peregrina, an egg-shaped pearl owned by Spanish queens and later bought by Richard Burton for Elizabeth Taylor, is arguably the most famous. The largest round pearl found sold for about a million dollars in 2014.
